summary: Watched since 1930, Garnet Mountain got its first permanent cab (a secondhand building from Lincoln Mountain) in 1950, replaced by the current R-6 cab in 1962, now a popular Forest Service rental.

facts.design: R-6 flat cab on a 10-foot concrete base

access.note: Reached via a 4.5-mile, 2,800-ft-gain trail in summer, or up to 10 miles of winter travel; rented year-round through Recreation.gov

visit.trail_note: Garnet Mountain Lookout Trail, 4.5 miles / 2,800 ft gain; motorized access on Rat Lake Trail June 16-Dec 1; winter requires ski/snowmobile/snowshoe up to 10 miles

events.note: Camp lookout (no permanent structure) established on the summit
First permanent structure: secondhand 2-story 9x9-ft frame cab moved from a Fish & Wildlife observatory on Lincoln Mountain
Current R-6 flat cab on 10-ft concrete base built, replacing the 1950 cab
Registered on the National Historic Lookout Register, April 12, 2022, as US 1535

evidence.supports: 1930 camp lookout, 1950 first permanent structure moved from Lincoln Mtn, 1962 current cab built, now rental
evidence.quote: Established with a camp lookout in 1930, the first permanent structure didn't arrive until 1950. The 2-story 9x9' frame cab was moved second-hand to the summit from a Fish & Wildlife observatory on Lincoln Mtn. In 1962, the present 10' concrete base with R-6 flat cab was built. The lookout is now on the rental program.

evidence.supports: same build history, confirms popularity on rental system
evidence.quote: Established with a camp lookout in 1930, the first permanent structure didn't arrive until 1950. The 2-story 9x9' frame cab was moved second-hand to the summit from a Fish & Wildlife observatory on Lincoln Mtn... The lookout is now on the Recreation Rental program, and is one of the most popular cabins on the rental system.

evidence.supports: elevation 8,245 ft, views of Spanish Peaks, Hyalite Ridge, Gallatin valley
evidence.quote: Garnet Mountain Fire Lookout sits on the apex of Garnet Mountain, at an elevation of 8,245 feet. The lookout provides a panoramic view of the surrounding peaks and valleys. Highlights include the Spanish Peaks to the west, the Gallatin Range to the south, the Hyalite Ridge to the east and the Gallatin River Valley to the north.

evidence.supports: grizzly bears, wolves, mountain lions, bighorn sheep present
evidence.quote: Grizzly bears are extremely common in this area, and gray wolves, mountain lions, deer, elk, moose, bighorn sheep and the Canada lynx also make their home here.

evidence.supports: 4.5-mile trail with 2,800-ft gain, motorized/winter access details
evidence.quote: The structure can be accessed by hiking, horseback or mountain bike on the Garnet Mountain Lookout Trail in the summer. The 4.5-mile trail gains 2,800 feet along its path. Motorcycles and ATVs can access the lookout via the Rat Lake Trail from June 16 through December 1. During winter months, guests must plan on skiing, snowmobiling or snowshoeing up to 10 miles.

evidence.supports: sleeps 4 on bunk beds, wood stove, no water/electricity, locked with combination sent ahead
evidence.quote: The lookout can sleep up to four people on provided bunk beds with mattresses. There is a wood stove for heat... Water and electricity are not available... The cabin remains locked; a combination lock code will be included in the reservation confirmation letter/email

notes_for_editor: No source gives an end date for staffed fire-watch duty, or names any specific fire spotted from Garnet Mountain. The brief's record flags a build-year conflict across sources, but all three sources checked here agree on the same build sequence (1930 camp / 1950 cab / 1962 cab), so no conflict was found in what we read; it's possible the flagged conflict is against a source not checked in this pass (e.g. an NRHP nomination). Fact-check 2026-10-04: the draft misstated Garnet Mountain as sitting 'in the Gallatin Range' -- source 2 lists the Gallatin Range only as a feature visible to the south, not the mountain's own range, so the story was corrected to list it alongside the other viewed features. Two footnote citations were also wrong: the 1950 secondhand-cab/Lincoln Mountain sentence had cited source 2 (Recreation.gov), which says nothing about that history, instead of source 3 (firelookout.com); and the 'one of the more popular lookouts' claim, which comes only from source 3's wording, had been attached to sources 1 and 2.
